notes.2: This question was well answered by the majority of candidates. Some candidates who chose to multiply by 3 at the start only multiplied two of the three terms, leading to a common incorrect answer of 3y – 5. Many candidates did not show any method, so if their answer was incorrect they were unable to earn any method marks. Answer: 3(y - 5)
notes.3: Part (b) was the least well answered part on the paper. In part (a), candidates were generally successful. The most common incorrect response was to shade only the set A. Part (b) caused problems for the vast majority of candidates and indicated that many were not confident with the set notation used in the question. A very common incorrect answer was 10. It was also common to see {3, 4, 7} as the final answer. Answers: (b) 14
notes.4: The responses to this question were an improvement on responses to similar questions set in previous years. The numbers 197.5 and 210.5 were observed on the majority of scripts. Some candidates, however, then proceeded to multiply the two numbers to find the area. Those candidates who did not use the correct figures usually used 197 and 210 or 197.4 and 210.4 or 197.49 and 210.49 Answer: 816
notes.5: Candidates were more successful at giving possible values for n than they were for a. It was common to see zero or a fraction being presented as a possible value for a. Some candidates gave a general solution for suitable values, similar to the mark scheme. Answer: a any negative integer, n any even (positive) integer
notes.6: Part (a) was generally well answered. A common error was to write the answer in standard form and then to round to three significant figures resulting in an incorrect final answer of 1.65×107. Part (b) was also generally well answered. In the cases where full marks were not gained it was quite common to see a correct value of 0.03317836 in the working but then the candidate proceeded to give incorrect answers of 3.3×10 −2, 3.31×10 −2 or 3.32×102. Answers: (a) 1.646×107 (b) 3.32×10 −2
notes.7: Part (a) was the best answered part on the paper and it was very rare to see an incorrect response. Part (b) was also well answered. The candidates who did not score full marks did not follow the instruction in the question to show all the steps in their working. The most common omission in the method was to show how 2 6 4 to get from × to . A very small number of candidates tried to use decimals and consequently scored 3 7 7 zero marks. Answers: (a) 36
notes.8: There was an excellent response to this question with most candidates scoring full marks. The majority of candidates chose to use the elimination method. The most common error when using the elimination method came from subtracting negatives. Some also did not multiply all three terms in an equation before eliminating one of the variables. The substitution method was a less popular choice of method and those that chose this method usually made an arithmetic error. Answer: x =5, y = −1
notes.9: This question was well answered. Most candidates multiplied 120 by 1.032, which frequently led to a correct answer. A small number of candidates used simple interest and consequently did not score any marks. Other common errors were not to give their answer to two decimal places as specified in the question, hence giving incorrect final answers of $127 or $127.308. Answer: 127.31
notes.10: The majority of candidates were able to write down a correct unsimplified equation. Only a small number were then unable to successfully solve their equation. The most common error came from incorrectly expanding 11(t +5) to give 11t +5. Answer: 120
notes.11: Those candidates who started with V =kL3 were usually successful. Some candidates who chose to start with V =kL3, however, then made an error by saying that 33 =9 leading to k =12 and then an incorrect final answer of 1500. It was also common to see an incorrect answer of 180, which was as a result of using direct proportion. Answer: 500
notes.12: This was a well answered question. In responses where full marks were not gained, 840 was nearly always evident in the working, sometimes followed by 840− x though this expression was then either multiplied by d or equated to d. 840− x Answer:
notes.13: Some of the candidates did not indicate their region with the letter R as stipulated in the question. (In such cases the worst unshaded region is marked, as this is a requirement of the syllabus for this topic.) A common incorrect response was to label the triangle in the centre as their region. Some candidates marked the R at the point of intersection of lines.
notes.14: Candidates made a better attempt at this question than to similar questions in previous years. The main errors seen were an incorrect gradient of and/or c = −1. Answer: y =4x +1
notes.15: The majority of candidates, who started with the correct formula, proceeded to successfully make r2 the subject of the formula, usually gaining full marks. A significant number of candidates were unable to write down the correct expression for the volume of a cylinder. Examples of incorrect expressions that were seen are 2πrh (curved surface area of a cylinder) and πr2h (volume of a cone). Occasionally a candidate showed no method and gave an answer of 4.9 cm which scored 0 marks. Answer: 4.94
notes.16: Most candidates started with an appropriate common denominator and then wrote down a correct numerator. Most errors came from incorrect expansion of brackets such as 2(x +2)+3(x −2)=2x +2+3x −2. Less common than in previous years was the incorrect cancellation of terms when a correct answer had been 5x−2/ 5x−1 written down e.g. = . x2 −4/ x2 −2 5x −2 Answer: (x −2)(x + 2)
notes.17: Part (a) was one of the best answered parts on the paper and it was very rare to see an incorrect answer. Candidates struggled in part (b) with many not recognising that the volume scale factor = (length scale factor)3. The most common incorrect answers were 800 (by incorrectly using a linear relationship) and 400 (by incorrectly using a square relationship). Some candidates tried to use the formula for the volume of a cylinder. Answers: (a) 4.5 (b) 200
notes.18: This question was generally well answered. Candidates were usually more successful with part (a) than with part (b). Common incorrect answers for part (a) were 3x9, 27x6 and 9x9. The most common incorrect answer for part (b) was 125x4. A minority of candidates left 33 and 52 in their answers. Answers: (a) 27x9 (b) 25x4
notes.19: Candidates were more successful with part (a) than with part (b). In part (a) most used the ratio correctly but some candidates converted 80 km to cm incorrectly, resulting in incorrect answers of 0.32 and 3.2. Part (b) was one of the less well answered questions on the paper. The usual error was not to take the square unit into account and to end up with an answer of 1.5 km. Other errors occurred from converting cm2 into km2 incorrectly with frequently seen incorrect answers of 375 and 3.75×1011. Answers: (a) 32 (b) 37.5
notes.20: This question was generally well answered with candidates being more successful in parts (a) and (b) than in parts (c) and (d). A common incorrect response to part (d) was 110o. Answers: (a) 35 (b) 55 (c) 55 (d) 125
notes.21: There were mixed responses to this question. Many candidates presented a correct efficient solution to the question, whilst some used correct but unnecessarily long methods. A significant number of candidates incorrectly took the perpendicular distance from M to BC to be 6 cm and then calculated the height of the triangle to be 42 +62 = 7.21 cm, thus giving a final answer of 123 cm2. Another commonly seen incorrect method was to say that the height of triangle BCP was 4 cm, thus giving a final answer of 84 cm2. A few candidates calculated ×(6×6)×4 i.e. the volume of the pyramid. Answer: 96
notes.22: Part (a) was better answered than in similar questions in previous years. The majority of candidates understood that to find the total distance travelled, they had to find the area under the speed-time graph. Most chose to use the area of two triangles plus the area of a rectangle rather than using the more efficient method of simply finding the area of the trapezium. A number of candidates made the error of omitting the ½ from the formula for the area of the second triangle. Another error was to use 50− 4= 45 for the base of the rectangle. In part (b)(i) a common error was to multiply by 60 instead of dividing by 60. Part (b)(ii) was one of the less well answered questions on the paper. The majority of the candidates knew that the numerical rise/run gave the acceleration during the first 4 minutes but they were unable to convert km/min2 to m/s2. Answers: (a) 159 (b)(i) 50 (b)(ii) 0.208
notes.key_messages:
To succeed in this paper candidates need to have completed full syllabus coverage, remember necessary
formulae, show all necessary working clearly and use a suitable level of accuracy.
notes.general_comments:
There was no evidence that candidates were short of time as almost all candidates were able to complete
the question paper and to demonstrate their knowledge and understanding. The occasional omissions were
due to difficulty with the questions rather than lack of time.
Candidates not giving answers to the correct degree of accuracy continued to be a concern this year. The
general rubric needs to be read carefully at the start of the examination and candidates need to ensure that
they have noted the accuracy requirements of particular questions in their checks at the end of the paper.
There were a significant number of candidates who did not use the available working space in the answer
booklet to show the necessary calculations for obtaining their answers. When there is only an incorrect
answer on the answer line and no relevant working the opportunity to earn method marks is lost.
